title: First words
goal: Greet people politely, say yes, no, thank you and sorry, and handle the first moments of a conversation in spoken Tamil.
intro:
Tamil greetings are simple and warm. **வணக்கம்** *vaṇakkam*, said with palms together, works for hello and goodbye at any time of day and with anyone.

From the very first lesson you will meet the two faces of Tamil: the **written** form you see on signs and in books, and the **spoken** form people actually use. Vocabulary is given in standard spelling with the spoken form in the notes; the phrases and dialogue are in everyday spoken Tamil.

grammar.title: Two Tamils: written and spoken
grammar.body:
Tamil is **diglossic**. The **written** language (செந்தமிழ் *centamiḻ*, 'refined Tamil') is used in books, newspapers, signs, news broadcasts and speeches. The **spoken** language (பேச்சுத் தமிழ் *pēcchu tamiḻ*) is what everybody uses with family, friends, in shops and in films. They share their words, but spoken Tamil shortens many endings.

You should **speak** spoken Tamil — using the written forms in conversation sounds stiff and bookish. But you need to **recognise** written forms to read. Throughout this course, vocab shows the standard spelling, and the note gives the spoken form when it differs. Some patterns you can already see:

நீங்கள் → நீங்க (*-gaḷ* → *-ga*)
இல்லை → இல்ல (final *-ai* → *-a*)
இருக்கிறேன் → இருக்கேன் (the present tense marker shrinks)
வேண்டாம் → வேணாம் (*ṇḍ* → *ṇ*)

grammar.title: Polite and informal 'you': நீங்க and நீ
grammar.body:
Tamil has two words for 'you'. **நீ** *nī* is intimate: use it with close friends of your age, younger siblings and children. **நீங்க** *nīnga* (written நீங்கள்) is polite, and is also the plural 'you all'. **As a learner, always use நீங்க** with adults you don't know well, elders, shopkeepers and officials.

The verb matches: polite verbs and requests end in **-ங்க** *-nga*: வாங்க 'come', உட்காருங்க 'sit', சொல்லுங்க 'tell'. The bare verb root (வா, சொல்லு) is the informal command and sounds rude to a stranger. This little -ங்க is the single most important politeness marker in spoken Tamil.

grammar.title: Word order: verb last
grammar.body:
Tamil puts the **verb at the end** of the sentence: subject – object – verb. 'I Tamil speak' rather than 'I speak Tamil'. Question words usually stay where the answer would go, and the subject is often dropped when the verb ending already shows who is meant (இருக்கேன் can only mean 'I am').

There are **no articles** ('a', 'the'); ஒரு *oru* 'one' is used when you really mean 'a'.

examples.en: I speak Tamil. (lit. I Tamil speak)
What did you say? (lit. you what said?)

dialogue.title: Meeting a neighbour
dialogue.setting: Anna, a newcomer to Chennai, meets her elderly neighbour Mr Rajan outside her flat in the morning.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.en: I'm fine, thank you. And you?

lines.speaker: Rajan
lines.en: I'm fine too. Have you eaten?

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.native: மன்னிச்சுக்கோங்க, எனக்குப் புரியல. கொஞ்சம் மெதுவா பேசுங்க.
lines.roman: mannicchukkōnga, enakku puriyala. konjam meduvā pēsunga.
lines.en: Sorry, I don't understand. Please speak a little slowly.

lines.speaker: Anna
lines.en: Ah, yes, I've eaten. Thank you very much.

culture: Tamils rarely say 'goodbye' in a final way: you say போயிட்டு வர்றேன் 'I'll go and come back', and the reply is போயிட்டு வாங்க. Asking சாப்பிட்டீங்களா? 'Have you eaten?' is a caring greeting, not an invitation. Older people often add -ம்மா (to women and girls) or -ப்பா (to men and boys) to soften what they say: சரிம்மா, வாப்பா. 'Thank you' is used less than in English among family and close friends, where it can even sound distant.
